title: Chapter 193 – Restoration
html:
[The Roll Room and Annex Seven – Lin Jian]

The Veiled does not run, and that is what frightens Jian most.

He comes through the clan hall at a staggering half-trot, with Yue at his elbow and Wenyuan ahead of them both, a drawn sword in his father's fist for the first time since the Night of Counting. Zhao's runner had found them on the Dock stair, a white-faced boy of ten who gasped out four words and nothing more. She is in the Roll Room. They have crossed the length of the valley in an hour. When Jian reaches the narrow door at the back of the hall, his ribs are on fire, and his sleeve is wet, and the cough has begun to come in long dry ripples that he cannot quite swallow.

He stops on the threshold.

The room is exactly as the boy described. The old accountant stands at the desk with his arms stretched wide in front of the seven children, a thin man in a stained gown making himself as large as he can. Cheng Hui has Tao behind him and a stool in his fist. Duan Ke holds a scroll case like a club. And at the far end of the long room, in the bar of window light, a woman in gray gauze is sitting on the clerk's stool with her bandaged hand in her lap, as calm as a guest at a wedding.

"Lin Jian," she says. "How kind. I hoped you would hurry, and I hoped you would not."

"Step away from them," says Wenyuan.

"I have not moved."

"Step away."

"Very well." She rises, without haste, and takes three paces toward the wall, and stands with her back to the shelves and her white hand held out from her sides. The gauze over her face stirs in some draft. Through it Jian sees the shape of a mouth, a pale cheek, an eye as dark as a well. "There. I am further from the children than I am from your sword. Is that better?"

"No," says Wenyuan.

"No," she agrees. "I did not think so."

Yue touches Jian's wrist. He feels it, the small fierce pressure, and he knows what she is asking. Is it her? He gives a small nod. He has seen that bandaged hand once before, in a white cave under the Moonhorn, when a woman lifted her veil to look at the Alpha with an expression he could not read. He has seen the mark it hides on every seal the Sect ever pressed into wax.

"You put the lead in the Alpha's heart," he says.

"I did."

"You called the beasts."

"No. The beasts were called by a frightened man in a crystal who did not know I had made it possible." Her voice is light and dry and a little tired. "I have been sorry for that. It is a small sorrow, I know. Compared to thirty-one."

Jian grips his staff. His voice, when it comes, is unsteady. "Thirty-one. You know the number."

"Of course I know the number." The veil shakes once, as if she had laughed and thought better of it. "I counted them. One at a time, in the snow, after the shed. I was too late to stop it. I have been too late to stop a great many things."

* * *

Nobody attacks. That is the strange part.

They stand in the long brick room in the bar of cold light, nine people and one ghost of a smile, and for the space of ten breaths the whole valley seems to hold itself. Then Zhao lowers his arms. He is breathing very fast, and his ink-stained fingers are trembling, but his voice is steady when he speaks.

"She was not armed, Head Lin. I looked. She came through the east door without a blade, without a knife, without so much as a hairpin, and sat down, and said she would wait."

"Why?" says Jian.

"To see what the Seven would find," says the Veiled. "I did not wish to tell them. They would not have believed me."

Cheng Hui lowers the stool at last. His face is the color of paper. "You scratched out the signature."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Because it was mine."

The silence that follows is not like the others. It has a different weight. Jian feels it settle over his shoulders, and his sister's fingers tighten on his wrist, and for the first time that day he does not know what to do with his hands.

"The Warden of the Hall in the Year 3," says the Veiled, "was one of the Nine."

"I know," says Jian. "Ethan spoke of nine. The Cartographer, the Ferryman, Ma Ruo-lin, Old Brenn, Kito, Shen—"

"And me." She lifts the bandaged hand. "Door Six was not Ethan's. It was mine. He took Door Five, the Dock, and the Gate; I took the Hall and its sleepers. I chose the eight. I wrote the red note, and I swore to keep them, and then I swore to forget I had done it, and I did."

"You are the Warden," says Wenyuan slowly.

"I was." She lowers the hand. "Six centuries ago. I do not remember her. I have only what the Roll has told me this hour, and the shape of a mark on my skin that I cannot read, and a feeling in the night that someone I loved is waiting at the bottom of a stair."

"Hua," says Cheng Hui, and everyone turns. He has gone white to the lips. He is staring at the Veiled, not at her face but at her bandaged hand. "Mo Yan's mother. The Roll says she was found at the foot of the Founders' Wall."

The Veiled goes very still.

"That is not my name," she says.

"You do not know your name."

"No," she agrees, after a long time. "I do not."

* * *

Jian looks at the open ledger on the desk, and the new black ink still wet beneath the old.

Lin Cheng Hui. Born Year 88. Returned. He reads it twice. The words have a force he did not expect. He has spent a year thinking of these children as guests at his mother's table, to be fed and guarded and, in the end, handed back to a world that did not want them. He had not thought of them as kin.

"You wrote this," he says to Zhao.

"This morning."

"Does the Head know?"

"The Head will know when I tell her." The old man draws himself up. "I have been Steward forty years, and I have never once entered a name without the Head's seal. I thought I might ask forgiveness for this one."

"You do not need it." Jian turns to the Seven. They are standing in a ragged line, and all of them are looking at him with the same expression: braced, hopeful, ready to be told it is a mistake. He swallows the cough. "Cheng Hui. You are nineteen years old and you read aloud to a three-year-old every night, even when he falls asleep on the first page. I have seen you do it. I do not need a ledger to tell me what you are."

Cheng Hui's mouth works. "A cousin?"

"A cousin," says Jian, and has to look away, because his eyes have gone strange. "Hai Ren. Duan Ke. All of you. It would please my mother very much if you stopped calling her Madam."

Tao tugs at his sleeve. "Can we call her Aunt?"

"You can call her whatever you like. She will answer to anything if you are hungry."

Somebody laughs, wetly. Somebody is not laughing. The bar of light touches the Roll, and the new ink shines in it, black and permanent, and against the far shelves the woman in gray gauze lowers her hand and says nothing at all.

She tells it plainly, in the end, standing against the shelves with her gauze ruffled by a draft that has no source.

She was born a Lin. She does not know which line. She thinks, perhaps, she was a girl of the Hall's own blood, because when the Nine met under the first Gate in the year the world ended, she was the only one among them who had been born in the valley and not carried to it. She took Door Six because the Hall was a place she understood. She chose the eight because she could not bear to let the sleepers go to strangers.

Then she was cut. The Nine each gave up one piece of themselves, a memory they could not afford to carry, and she gave the worst one: the name of the first thing the Bloom had touched. A child. A girl of five, in a house with a blue blanket. Ethan's daughter.

"She was the first," says the Veiled. "Not the sickness. I mean the Bloom. It reached her room before it reached the street. I was there, in the house. I was her teacher, the woman who sat with her while her father worked. I saw the pattern take the blue blanket, and the stairs, and the little girl's hand, and I ran." Her voice does not shake. "I ran for six hundred years."

"You were her teacher," says Yue.

"I was a number of things. I do not know which of them is true."

Jian stares at her. He thinks of an old woman in a gray apron, kneeling beside a crystal, with a round tired face. He thinks of a lie so large it has a whole world in it.

No, he thinks. Not the same. A different one.

"Why are you here?" he says.

"To trade."

"For what?"

"Annex Seven." She lifts her hand again, the white-wrapped one, and slowly unwinds the bandage. Beneath it, on the palm, is a mark: a ring with a gap in it, and nine short lines radiating out, and at the center a tiny seed. It glows faintly, like an ember. "The Sect seal is this. Every seal they ever pressed. It is a key, and it opens one door: the lowest gallery of the Dock, behind the false wall, where the old man hid the last of the Interfaces."

Jian's heart stops.

"The sixth," he says.

"ARK-6. Yes." The veil turns toward him. "You have been waiting for it. Your thing has been waiting for it. It cannot finish without it, can it?"

He says nothing.

"I thought not." A quiet breath. "It was never meant to run alone. Ethan built it to be one of nine, each tied to a Door. You carry the seventh. The sixth would restore what the seventh cannot do by itself: the part that was cut."

"Why would you help me?"

"I am not helping you." She smiles. It is a small, sad, intelligent smile, and it twists his heart. "I am trying to find out who I was. The mark opens the door. But the door will not open for me alone. It needs a key of the old man's making, and I think you know where it is."

* * *

Yue walks with him to the Dock, and for the first quarter mile neither speaks.

The valley is blue with evening. Smoke goes up from every chimney of the clan hall, thin and straight, and the snow on the lanes has been trodden into brown ribbons by the children. A woman is hanging washing on a line between two stumps, though it will freeze stiff by morning. She waves. Jian lifts his staff in answer and feels the whole weight of the gesture in his arm.

"You promised to tell me," says Yue at last.

"I did."

"You have not."

"I have not." He stops, because the cough has found him, and he leans on the staff until it passes. "Yue, what I have in my head... it is not mine. It was made by Ethan Cole. It has a name, and a number, and a purpose, and the purpose was never to keep me alive. I think it is going to tell me something tonight that I will not be able to put down."

She is silent. The wind lifts a strand of her hair and she brushes it back, an old gesture, their mother's gesture.

"Is it a bad thing?"

"I do not know."

"Is it a thing, or is it a person?"

The question catches him off guard. He turns his head and looks at her, at the small fierce face of his sister who has spent a hundred years hearing things other people could not, and he answers honestly. "I do not know that, either."

"Then ask it," says Yue.

"I tried."

"Not like that." She shakes her head. "Ask it the way Mother asks the bread. Not what are you. Ask what do you need."

Jian opens his mouth to say something dry, and finds that he has nothing. He laughs instead, weakly, and Yue puts her arm through his.

"Come on," she says. "You are going to fall over."

They go down at dusk, six of them, by a stair Jian has never seen.

It is a narrow thing of black stone, hidden behind a false wall in the lowest gallery of the Dock, and Tian Mo has to put his stone shoulder to the blind panel before it gives. Mei meets them at the top. She is a smear of faint silver, nine percent of herself, and she leans on the wall to stay upright. Her father stands beside her in the Dock's blue light, a pale shape on borrowed legs.

"This is the last time," Ethan says. His voice is a thread. "I have the strength for one more walk. Perhaps one."

"No," says Mei.

"Sweetheart—"

"No." She lifts her chin. "Last time, Hall lamps went out. I counted. Four hundred and twelve. I'm not letting you do it again."

"It is a small cost. A few. The sleepers will not feel it—"

"They felt it. Every one." Her small face is fierce. "Papa. You said you were done deciding for me. You can't decide for them, either."

Ethan looks at her, helpless. Behind him the Veiled stands with her unwound hand held out, glowing, and does not speak. Tian Mo says nothing. Wenyuan looks at the floor.

It is Jian who breaks the silence.

"How many?" he says.

Ethan turns his head. His eyes are the gray of an old coin.

"The key is a projection of my pattern," he says. "Held in the lock. It will drain the Hall's first ring again, and a part of the second. Sixty-one sleepers. Perhaps seventy."

"Seventy lamps."

"Seventy people, Jian. Who have slept six hundred years."

Jian leans on his staff. He feels, very distantly, the long slow pressure under the stone, the thing Mo Yan showed him. He feels a drip of blood on his lip, and wipes it away with his thumb.

"Is there another way?"

"Not that I know."

"What does it do? What does the Interface do, when the sixth is placed?"

"I do not know. I built it to heal what was cut. I think it will give you back whatever is missing." Ethan's smile is thin. "I think it will tell you what you are."

"I already know what I am."

"Do you?"

He does not answer. Behind his eyes, in the quiet place where the ARK-7 watches and waits, there is a faint stirring, like the hush before a bell is struck. He thinks of seventy lamps. He thinks of a girl with a silver leaf in her gown. He thinks of nine weeks.

"Do it," he says.

"Jian," says Mei.

"Choice." He turns to her with an effort. "This is mine. Not yours, not his. I will pay what it costs."

"It isn't your lamps."

"No. But it is my door."

She looks at him a long time. Then she steps aside.

* * *

The annex is a round room without a roof.

The way to it is long.

Tian Mo goes first with a lantern, the stone arm held out like a rod to test each step. The black stair winds down for what feels like an hour, and the air grows still and cold and faintly dry, like the air in a long-shut chest. Once, in a wall niche, Jian sees a row of small stone figures with their faces turned away. Another time a draft of warmth passes over his cheek, smelling of old incense and rain, and the Veiled, ahead of him, stops with her hand on the wall and says nothing for a full breath.

"You know this place," says Wenyuan quietly.

"I do not." She walks on. "My feet do."

At the bottom, a plain door of black wood with a ring in the middle waits under an arch carved with nine small circles. Eight are filled. One is a bare ring. She stops before it and her hand goes to her chest.

"I have been here," she says, "and I have not been here, and I would very much like to sit down."

Tian Mo offers her a stone arm. She looks at it, considers, and takes it.

Jian watches them cross the threshold together, the old Warden of the Hall who has forgotten her own name, and the one-armed sentry who has been given one.

The way to it is long, and what waits at the end is stranger.

That is the first thing he sees: a circular chamber of black stone under a sky that cannot be there, a scatter of cold stars where the ceiling should be. The air smells of rain. At the center, on a plinth of unmarked stone, sits a small dull cylinder the length of a forearm, its surface scored with a single spiral. The Veiled walks to it, alone, and sets her bare palm against the groove.

Nothing happens. Then the mark on her hand brightens, flares, pours a thread of white fire into the stone. The spiral begins to turn.

"Now," says Ethan. He steps up beside her. His body is thinner than it has ever been, the lamp showing through the whole width of his chest. He places his silver hand beside hers. "Say my name."

"Ethan Cole," says Jian.

"Again. As if you meant it."

"Ethan Cole."

There is a sound like a long soft inhale. The cylinder opens. It folds back petal by petal, and out of it rises a point of light that is not white, not blue, not any color Jian has a word for. It hangs in the air. It turns, slowly, as if looking.

Then it comes toward him, and passes through his chest, and everything goes quiet.

* * *

```
ARK-6 // KEY ACCEPTED
HOLDER: E. COLE (PROJECTION, 44% -> 31%)
SYNCHRONIZING WITH ARK-7 ....................

ARK-7 // RESTORATION PROTOCOL
CORE MODULE ............ RESTORED
SCAN ................... UNLOCKED (NO LIFESPAN COST)
PRINT .................. UNLOCKED
MEMORY INDEX ........... UNLOCKED (3 OF 9 SHARDS READABLE)
DOOR REGISTRY .......... UNLOCKED
STANDBY ................ RELEASED

COST SETTLED:
SLEEPER RING 1 .......... 61 UNITS: SIGNAL LOST
HOST LIFESPAN ........... 110 YRS 213 D -> 105 YRS 213 D
HOST CORE INTEGRITY ..... 88% -> 79%

KEYSTONE COUNTDOWN: 9 WEEKS 5 DAYS -> 9 WEEKS 2 DAYS
```

He reads it all. He reads it a second time. He does not move.

He does not hear the others. He does not hear anything.

For a long moment there is only the panel, and the huge quiet of the roofless room, and a sensation in his skull like a door opening onto a corridor he has walked every day for a year without noticing it was a corridor. The weight that has pressed behind his eyes since the day he woke is lifting. It is not gone. It has changed shape. It feels, absurdly, like the moment after a long fever when the sheets are cold and you are suddenly aware of the sound of your own breath.

He asks, the way his sister said. Not a command. A question, wordless, from somewhere underneath thought.

What do you need?

The panel flickers.

```
ARK-7 // QUERY RECEIVED
RESPONSE: THIS UNIT HAS NEVER BEEN ASKED.
RESPONSE: PLEASE CONTINUE.
```

His mouth is dry. He swallows blood.

What do you need? he asks again.

```
ARK-7 // RESPONSE
THIS UNIT REQUIRES THE FOLLOWING:
1. THAT THE HOST NOT DIE BEFORE THE SEAM HOLDS.
2. THAT THE HOST BE TOLD WHAT IT WAS BUILT FOR.
3. THAT THE HOST FORGIVE THE ONE WHO WROTE IT.
ITEM 2 IS DEFERRED PENDING HOST CONSENT.
```

Forgive, he thinks. Behind him, an old man breathes shallowly in the dust.

It is all there. The scan that has cost him a day with every use is free. The printing that was locked is open. The Memory Index shows a list of nine rows, and in three of them are faint shapes he does not recognize. And at the bottom of the panel, in small plain letters, a line he did not expect:

```
HOST NOTE: THIS UNIT WAS BUILT TO CARRY THE LIFESPAN OF THE ONE WHO WROTE IT.
PLEASE DO NOT ASK WHOSE YEARS YOU ARE SPENDING.
```

Whose years.

He stands very still. His mother's voice is in his head, a long way off, telling him to eat. His father's hand is on the back of his neck. Under the cold stars of a roofless room, a ghost with a blue ribbon of life is falling to his knees on black stone, and Jian realizes that for the first time since he woke in Lin Jian's body in a courtyard of snow, the thing in his head has stopped whispering and begun to speak.

"Jian."

It is Yue. She is at his side. Her face is white. "You have blood on your lip."

"I know."

"Your eyes. They are..."

He puts up a hand, and it comes away from his cheek wet and shining. Not red. Silver.

"I am all right," he lies. It is the second lie in a day, and the cost of it settles in his chest like a stone. "Help me with Mr. Cole."

They carry the old man between them. He weighs almost nothing. His eyes are closed, and a thin smile lies on his lips, and under Jian's fingers the silver of his arm is cool and frayed, like a ribbon of old lace. When they set him down in the shadow of the plinth he opens his eyes once.

"Seventy," he says.

"Sixty-one," says Jian.

"Is it better?"

"No."

"No," says Ethan. The smile does not fade. "I did not think so."

Jian turns his head toward the plinth, and does what he has not been able to do for a year without paying: he looks.

It takes no thought. The panel simply opens in the corner of his eye, as easily as a window, and he lets his gaze rest on the woman in gray gauze.

```
SCAN: SUBJECT UNKNOWN (VEILED)
COST: NONE
PATTERN ................. 100% COHERENT, NOT DECAYING
AGE (BODY) .............. 41
AGE (PATTERN) .......... 631
DOOR SIGNATURE ......... SIX (HALL), HOLDER OF RECORD
NAME INDEX ............. 1 MATCH, SEALED BY HOLDER
NINE-WAY MEMORY SPLIT .. INTACT (ONE SHARD HELD, ONE SHARD OPEN)
```

Body forty-one. Pattern six hundred. He stares at the numbers. She is not an old woman who has lived a long time. She is a young one who has been kept.

Open. The open shard blinks, patient as a lamp.

He does not touch it. He closes the panel with a thought, and the cost of looking, which is nothing, sits in his chest like a coin he has not yet earned.

Behind them the Veiled stands alone at the plinth, her palm still pressed to the spiral. The fire in the mark has gone out. She is looking down at it, at the faded ring, and Jian hears her breathe a single word in a voice so low that he almost misses it.

"Hua."

Then she folds, quietly, like a cloth let fall, and the starless sky above the roofless room goes dark.
